25 A car travelling in a straight line at a speed of 30 m s–1 passes near a stationary observer while
sounding its horn. The true frequency of sound from the horn is 400 Hz.
The speed of sound in air is 336 m s–1.
What is the change in the frequency of the sound heard by the observer as the car passes?
A
39 Hz
B
66 Hz
C
72 Hz
D
78 Hz

hints: Notice the observer hears a higher pitch while the $30 \text{m s}^{-1}$ car approaches and a lower pitch after it passes, so you need two observed frequencies.
Recall the moving-source Doppler formula $f_o = f_s v/(v \pm v_s)$ with $v = 336 \text{m s}^{-1}$, using minus for approach and plus for recession.
Calculate both $400 \times 336/306$ and $400 \times 336/366$ in $\text{Hz}$, then subtract the lower heard frequency from the higher one.
walkthrough: Identify the data: source frequency $f_s = 400 \text{Hz}$, wave speed $v = 336 \text{m s}^{-1}$, source speed $v_s = 30 \text{m s}^{-1}$, observer stationary.
State the Doppler rule for a moving source: wavefronts are crowded ahead and spread behind, so $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$ on approach and $f_o = f_s v/(v + v_s)$ on recession.
Find the change heard as the car passes by subtracting: $\Delta f = 439.2 - 367.2 \approx 72 \text{Hz}$.

A.explanation: This is only the increase on approach, $439 \text{Hz} - 400 \text{Hz} \approx 39 \text{Hz}$, not the full high-to-low change as the car passes.

B.explanation: This is close to twice the drop below $400 \text{Hz}$ on recession, and does not equal the observed approaching frequency minus the receding frequency.

C.explanation: The difference between the approaching frequency of about $439 \text{Hz}$ and the receding frequency of about $367 \text{Hz}$ is about $72 \text{Hz}$.

D.explanation: This is about twice the approaching shift of $39 \text{Hz}$, which incorrectly assumes the fall below $400 \text{Hz}$ equals the rise above it.
